hook_clip: Claude built this capacity planner from one written spec.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: Can it replace Float? The spec copies the part of Float a small studio needs. Each person's working days and hours. Company holidays and time off. Projects with phases and budgets in hours. And bookings by the week, confirmed or tentative.

The core rule is one calculation, done the same way on every screen. A person's real capacity for a week is their working hours, minus holidays and time off. Booked hours are set against it. A week that goes over is flagged Over. A week that only goes over if tentative work goes ahead is flagged Tentative over. And overbooking is a warning, never a refusal.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation. Capacity, bookings and the schedule. Projects, budgets and who has time. Then notifications and export. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser.
cues: Projects, budgets and who has time

scenes.text: Here's what it built. The schedule flags Lee Park at forty of thirty-six hours, and Maya Chen tentatively over from the thirtieth. Priya's Thanksgiving week shows twelve hours of capacity, with the holiday counted once. Before you save a booking, the preview warns that Sam Okafor would be over by twenty hours. The Brightline project shows five hundred and sixty-four hours booked against a five hundred and thirty hour budget. Who has time for UI design puts Jo Park first, with twenty-four hours free. And on a phone, the name column stays put while the weeks scroll.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all thirty-three checks passed, along with two hundred and twenty-two automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The test build exposed eighty-nine places where Claude had to guess. Nothing said whether someone you deactivate stays signed in. The spec's own example said a phase had six bookings, but the seed data gave it five. And nothing said what happens when two time off entries cover the same day. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't production-ready. Production sign-in, real email delivery, hosting, clock changes and two planners saving at the same moment were never tested. Check those yourself before your team relies on it.

So is it worth building? Float's Starter plan costs seven dollars per scheduled person a month, billed yearly, so ten people pay eight hundred and forty dollars a year. Pro is twelve dollars. Build it if you plan a small team by the week and mainly need to know who is free. Buy it if you need time tracking, rates and margins, or holiday calendars for several offices.
Everything is in one file. The data model, thirteen rules, the seed data, four phase prompts and thirty-three checks, with all eighty-nine fixes included.
